narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. By far the strongest influence was your third-year class ranking. Placing in the bottom decile of your class sent a very strong signal toward failure, outweighing most other information the model considered. Your first-year ranking also mattered, though less dramatically; sitting in the fourth decile rather than the sixth-decile average of accepted students added a modest push in the same negative direction.

Your family’s lower-middle income bracket was the third most important factor. While this feature pulled slightly toward a passing outcome compared with the typical accepted student (most of whom come from upper-middle or middle brackets), its helpful effect was far too small to offset the academic signals.

Taken together, these pieces of information led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. To improve your chances on a future application, focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing in law school if you are already enrolled, or consider retaking the LSAT and raising your undergraduate GPA before reapplying. Demonstrating clear upward progress in your grades will be the most powerful way to change this prediction. (218 words)
